\chapter{Muy --- The Same Word, Bitten Short}
\label{ch:muy}
\hlchaptermodality{226}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that something is very something.}

I can say that something is very something.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[muy]{muy — the same word, bitten short}

\label{lesson:ES-C60-muy}



\begin{quote}
You have said \emph{mucho} since chapter six — \emph{mucho gusto}.

Now you want to say that something is \textbf{very} something. \emph{Cansado} is tired; how do you say \emph{very tired}?
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\emph{Estoy} \emph{\textbf{muy}} \emph{cansado.}
\end{quote}

\textbf{muy} is not a new word to learn. It is \emph{\textbf{mucho}}, with its ending bitten off. Both are Latin \emph{\textbf{multum}}, \emph{much} — one kept whole, one worn short.

Spanish does this a lot: a long form for standing alone, a short form for leaning on the word after it. You will meet the same trick again in this chapter's neighbours.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
The two shapes are not interchangeable, and the rule is easy because the word tells you itself.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{\textbf{mucho}} \emph{café} & in front of a \textbf{noun} — the long form \\
\emph{\textbf{muy}} \emph{grande} & in front of an \textbf{adjective} — the short one \\
\emph{\textbf{muy}} \emph{bien} & in front of an \textbf{adverb} — the short one \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So \emph{muy} never stands alone. If somebody asks how you are and you want to say \emph{very}, you cannot answer \emph{muy} — there is nothing for it to lean on. You would answer \emph{muy bien}.

And this is the strongest \emph{very} Spanish has in one word. \emph{Muy grande} is as big as \emph{grande} gets without reaching for another sentence.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{muy bien}, \emph{muy grande}, \emph{muy cansado}
  \item \emph{mucho café}, then \emph{muy grande}, and hear which is which
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Long form or short form in front of an adjective? (\textbf{Short} — \emph{muy}.)

And how many Latin words are \emph{muy} and \emph{mucho} between them? (\textbf{One} — \emph{multum}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
